bugs.summary: isGeneric(f=) and isGeneric(f=, fdef=) behave inconsistently for primitive functions
bugs.creator: jaganmn2

comments.creator: jaganmn2
comments.text:
An issue related to but different from Bug 18369.

Another aspect of `isGeneric` behaviour where clarification is needed concerns default and non-default methods for internally generic primitive functions.  Comments in the source code suggest that only non-default methods should affect the result.

```
    ## check primitives. These are never found as explicit generic functions.
    if(isBaseFun(fdef)) {
        if(is.character(f) && f %in% "as.double") f <- "as.numeric"
        ## the definition of isGeneric() for a base function is that methods are defined
        ## (other than the default primitive)
        gen <- genericForBasic(f, mustFind = FALSE)
        return(is.function(gen) && length(names(.getMethodsTable(gen))) > 1L)
    }
```

However, the documentation does not distinguish between default and non-default methods.

> A call to `isGeneric` tells you whether methods have been defined for this primitive function, anywhere in the current search list, or in the specified position `where`.

The implementation is itself inconsistent.  Specifically, calls `isGeneric(f=, fdef=)` analyze the method table, while calls `isGeneric(f=)` do not, leading to inconsistent results.  Consider any internally generic primitive function whose generic "proxy" is not already cached in `methods:::.genericTable` at start-up (because no methods for that function or its "group" are defined by **methods** itself).

```
> exists("sum", envir = methods:::.genericTable, inherits = FALSE)
[1] FALSE
```

The formal generic function object is defined in `methods:::.BasicFunsList` with a method table containing only a default method.  This object is not yet cached in `methods:::.genericTable`.

```
> fn <- methods:::.BasicFunsList[["sum"]]
> is(fn, "genericFunction")
[1] TRUE
> mt <- environment(fn)[[".MTable"]]
> names(mt)
[1] "ANY"
> identical(mt[["ANY"]], sum)
[1] TRUE
```

At this point, `sum` is not generic by any definition employed by `isGeneric`.  There is no such object in `.genericTable` (consulted by `.getGenericFromCache`) and the object in `.BasicFunsList` (consulted by `genericForBasic`) has no non-default methods in its method table.

```
> isGeneric("sum")
[1] FALSE
> isGeneric("sum", fdef = sum)
[1] FALSE
```

Now call `getGeneric("sum")`, which has the side effect of caching the object from `.BasicFunsList` in `.genericTable`.

```
> identical(getGeneric("sum"), fn)
[1] TRUE
> exists("sum", envir = methods:::.genericTable, inherits = FALSE)
[1] TRUE
> identical(methods:::.genericTable[["sum"]], fn)
[1] TRUE
```

It is still the case that only a default method is defined for `sum`.

```
> names(environment(fn)[[".MTable"]])
[1] "ANY"
```

But now the first usage of `isGeneric` gives a different answer.

```
> isGeneric("sum")
[1] TRUE
> isGeneric("sum", fdef = sum)
[1] FALSE
```

Hence we should decide what is really meant (in the help page) by "whether methods have been defined for this primitive function" and patch `isGeneric` to employ this definition more rigorously.

(Initially, ..) I agree this is a bug,
and I think `isGeneric()` should try harder before saying `FALSE`.
As you showed, it _could_  call `getGeneric(*, mustWork=FALSE)` which I think should always return `NULL` if it doesn't find anything.
If it does find something, almost surely  `isGeneric()` should return `TRUE` immediately.
One could think of trying a more efficient version of `getGeneric()`, e.g.,
possible `{methods}` own hidden `.getGeneric()`.

**However**, I wrote the above before carefully rereading the subsection for `isGeneric` inside the `help(isGeneric)` section `Summary of Functions:`  which 
ends with the paragraph

>  The behavior of `isGeneric` and getGeneric for primitive
>  functions is slightly different.  These functions don't exist
>  as formal generic function objects (for efficiency and
>  historical reasons), regardless of whether methods have been
>  defined for them.  For a primitive function, `isGeneric`
>  tests whether non-default methods have been defined, whereas
>  getGeneric returns what the formal generic function object
>  would be, even if no methods have been defined.

I'm concluding from this that both functions behave as they do (well, "almost", see below), on purpose.


When you  say
> Now call `getGeneric("sum")`, which has the side effect of caching the
> object from `.BasicFunsList` in `.genericTable`.

and use

```
> identical(getGeneric("sum"), fn)
[1] TRUE
> exists("sum", envir = methods:::.genericTable, inherits = FALSE)
[1] TRUE
> identical(methods:::.genericTable[["sum"]], fn)
[1] TRUE
```
> 
> It is still the case that only a default method is defined for `sum`.

you are right,  and given the documentation above, `isGeneric("sum")` becoming `TRUE` is actually wrong.
As you mention, the `getGeneric()` *does* cache it in `.genericTable` which may be the bug here:
If we want to keep the documented behaviour it should only cache it when  isGeneric() is TRUE (or _"would be true"_, if there's an easier way to check that).


Note the 2nd to last line, when the result of `getGeneric()` is printed:
```
> getGeneric(sum)
standardGeneric for "sum" defined from package "base"
  belonging to group(s): Summary 

function (x, ..., na.rm = FALSE) 
standardGeneric("sum", .Primitive("sum"))
<bytecode: 0xe807440>
<environment: 0xe805a30>
Methods may be defined for arguments: x, na.rm
Use  showMethods(<pkg>:::sum)  for currently available ones where <pkg> does not seem to be among the loadedNamespaces().
> 
```
i.e., the `show()` method __does__ note that it cannot find any S4 methods (in the current R session with the currently loaded namespaces).

.. of course, the further complication (also mentioned by the show() method) is that `sum` is part of the groupGeneric `"Summary"`,
and after, e.g.,  `loadNamespace("Matrix")` the output above would not change, but of course  `sum(<..Matrix>)` would use S4 methods from the Matrix package, and indeed,  `showMethods(Summary)`  will show them.

comments.text:
My patch for Bug 18369 may have confused this issue a bit.  In R-patched, the paragraph concerning primitive functions reads:

> The behavior of `isGeneric` and `getGeneric` for primitive functions is slightly different.  These functions don't exist as formal function objects (for efficiency and historical reasons), regardless of whether methods have been defined for them.  A call to 'isGeneric' tells you whether **methods** have been defined for this primitive function, anywhere in the current search list, or in the specified position 'where'.  In contrast, a call to 'getGeneric' will return what the generic for that function would be, even if no methods have been currently defined for it.

In R-devel, it now reads:

> The behavior of `isGeneric` and `getGeneric` for primitive functions is slightly different.  These functions don't exist as formal generic function objects (for efficiency and historical reasons), regardless of whether methods have been defined for them.  For a primitive function, `isGeneric` tests whether **non-default methods** have been defined, whereas `getGeneric` returns what the formal generic function object would be, even if no methods have been defined.

I added the qualifier "non-default" so that the documentation would align with the intention of the source code, which is reflected in the comments there.  But that was *before* I detected *this* bug which reveals that the implementation does not consistently behave "as intended", i.e., does not consistently consult the method table and distinguish between default and non-default methods.

Hence it seems that there is an opportunity here to decide between two paths:

* Eliminate from the paragraph the qualifier "non-default", which did not exist before.  Then have `isGeneric` behave as you suggested: `isGeneric(f)` tests whether `getGeneric(f)` is non-`NULL`, without consulting the method table.
* Keep the qualifier "non-default", respecting the intention of the original source code.  Then have `isGeneric` consult the method table in all cases.

In my opinion, the first approach is both more intuitive and more useful, because then `isGeneric(f)` can then be used as a test of whether `setGeneric(f)` or `setMethod(f)` would create a new generic function object.  The second approach is confusing to me because the distinction between default and non-default methods seems arbitrary.

Another complication, relevant the above discussion but perhaps not affecting primitive functions: Should `isGeneric` (gain an option to) consider implicit generic functions?  It is possible (e.g., for `f = "qr.X"`) that `getGeneric(f)` is `NULL` but `implicitGeneric(f)` is non-`NULL`.

Since the patch for bug 18369 has been backported, R-patched now has the word "non-default" in `help("isGeneric")`.  I mention it mainly for anyone now confused by my comment 2.

We should decide on a resolution here before R 4.4.3 is released in the spring.
